newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FOCUS-Pakistan's Leghari in limelight after sacking PM.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pakistan's Leghari in limelight after sacking PM.

text.p: President Farooq Leghari, who ordered Monday's Pakistan elections after sacking former ally Benazir Bhutto as prime minister, is a feudal landowner with a strong Moslem faith.
For three years after he was elected president the tall Leghari maintained a figurehead role and made no effort to wield the sweeping constitutional powers he had spoken against.

But on November 5 he used those powers to dissolve the National Assembly (lower house), dismiss Bhutto's three-year-old government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, and order new elections.
Bhutto lambasted Leghari for what she saw as an act of treachery, but the president won praise from her political foes.
The Oxford-educated tribal chief from Punjab province began his five-year presidential term in November 1993, a month after Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) won an election.
The former secretary-general of the PPP was the party's choice as presidential candidate.
An ethnic Baloch from Dera Ghazi Khan in rural Punjab, he speaks Balochi, Pashtu, Punjabi, Urdu and English. A keen hunter and hill-walker, he is married with two sons and two daughters.

After sacking Bhutto, Leghari chose a caretaker cabinet to oversee the polls, launch an anti-corruption drive and reform the economy, but it has made little headway in bringing corruption charges against top politicians.

The president ran into criticism when he set up a Council for National Defence and Security on January 6 under his own chairmanship, giving the armed forces' chiefs a formal advisory role in government for the first time.

Defence Minister Shahid Hamid commented that the president was no longer simply a titular head of state, giving ammunition to critics who accused Leghari of using constitutional trickery to tilt power towards the presidency and the military.
Pakistan has been under military rule for nearly half of the 50 years since its creation in 1947.

Leghari brushed aside questions as to why formation of such a council could not be left to the next government. "What is necessary to be done today has to be done today," he said. "Why are people so afraid? Why are they afraid of the president?"
Bhutto now calls Leghari "Farooq-ul-Haq" after Pakistan's late military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq.
"What a pity for him that he can't declare himself chief of army staff. Otherwise I am sure he will put on a uniform and do that too," she scoffed last month.

After he became president, Leghari spoke against the presidential power to dissolve the National Assembly, a prerogative that derives from an amendment inserted in the constitution by General Zia in 1985.
"The Sword of Damocles hanging over the parliament of presidential dissolution must be removed," he said. "I feel I can play a crucial role in stabilising democracy."

The PPP and its main rival, the Pakistan Muslim League (PML), both oppose the amendment, used to throw out four elected governments in eight years, but have never cooperated to provide the two-thirds majority in the house needed to undo it.
Leghari, while remaining loyal to Bhutto, weathered early opposition attacks on his integrity and impartiality.
The PML had accused the president, one of the few Pakistani politicians widely seen as honest, of selling land to the collapsed Mehran Bank at inflated prices. Leghari denied the charge.
The opposition campaign climaxed in October 1994 when PML deputies shouted him down at the formal opening of parliament.
